title: Spot the broken max
idea: TOOL: recognise common mistakes in the best-so-far pattern (wrong start, wrong comparison, backwards assignment).

exercises.prompt:
This is meant to find the biggest, but it is broken:

nums = [-3, -1, -7]
best = 0
for n in nums:
    if n > best:
        best = n
print(best)

What prints, and why is it wrong?
options: 0 — no negative beats 0, so best never updates to a real value
exercises.explanation: Starting at 0 is the bug: no negative is bigger than 0, so best stays 0 — which isn't even in the list. Start at nums[0] instead.

exercises.prompt: What is the fix for the code above?
exercises.explanation: Starting best at the first real value lets negatives be compared properly. Then it finds -1 correctly.

options: The comparison is < — that finds the smallest, not the biggest
exercises.explanation: < keeps the smallest. To find the biggest you need >. (That < version is exactly how you'll find the minimum next unit — hold that thought.)

options: The assignment is backwards — it should be best = n
exercises.explanation: 'n = best' overwrites the bigger value and loses it. The winner must be saved INTO best: 'best = n'.

exercises.prompt: Forgetting to indent the 'best = n' line under the if would change what the code does.
exercises.explanation: If 'best = n' is not indented under the if, it runs every pass and best becomes the LAST value, not the biggest. Indentation controls what belongs to the if.

exercises.prompt: If 'best = n' runs on every pass (not guarded by the if), what does best end up holding for [4, 9, 2]?
exercises.explanation: Without the if guard, best is overwritten every time and keeps only the last value, 2. The if is what makes it the biggest.

exercises.prompt: A learner starts best at the list's LENGTH: best = len(nums). Why is that a bad start for a max?
options: Length has nothing to do with the values — it can be bigger or smaller than them by accident
exercises.explanation: The starting best must be a real value from the list. len() is a count of items, unrelated to how big the values are.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are correct ways to find the biggest? (pick all)
options: start best at nums[0], replace when n > best
start best at nums[0], replace when n >= best
start best at 0, replace when n > best
start best at len(nums), replace when n > best
exercises.explanation: Both nums[0] starts work (> and >= land on the same max). Starting at 0 or at len() can give a value that isn't even in the list.

exercises.prompt: You test your max code only on [1, 2, 3] (already sorted up) and it works. Why is that a weak test?
options: A rising list hides bugs — the biggest is conveniently last; test unsorted and negative lists too
It is actually a perfect test
exercises.explanation: A rising list makes almost any buggy approach look right. Test with the biggest in the middle, with ties, and with negatives to really check it.

exercises.prompt: A good habit is to test max code on a list whose biggest value is NOT the first or last item.
exercises.explanation: Putting the biggest in the middle catches starts and comparisons that only work by luck on sorted lists.
